EMPIRICAL RESEARCH PLAN  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. IDENTIFICATION STRATEGY  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Strategy: Staggered-adoption Difference-in-Differences (DID) complemented by an event-study.  

Why it fits:  
• Treatment (first CHC grant) arrives in different counties at different calendar years (1965-1974, then 1975-1980 “late adopters”).  
• We observe a balanced county×year mortality panel from 1959–1988, giving ≥ 6 pre-years and up to 24 post-years for every cohort of adopters.  
• The contemporaneous CHC grant process is described by historians as “chaotic” and “advocate-driven,” suggesting quasi-random timing once we condition on baseline county attributes and national shocks.  
• DID allows us to difference out common, nationwide mortality trends (e.g., medical technology, smoking) with year FEs; county FEs absorb time-invariant differences in health endowments.  
• The event-study (Sun & Abraham 2021 / Callaway & Sant’Anna 2021) checks pre-trends and accommodates treatment-effect heterogeneity.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. TREATMENT AND CONTROL  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
TREAT_it = 1 iff county i has at least one operating Community Health Center in calendar year t; 0 otherwise.  
(Secondary: number of CHC FTE physicians per 10 000 pop.)

Treatment timing  
G_i = first fiscal year a CHC grant is awarded in county i. Event-time k = t – G_i (k = 0 is first full calendar year with a CHC).  

Control group  
(i) “Never-treated” counties: no CHC by 1980.  
(ii) “Not-yet-treated” counties serve as additional controls prior to adoption (“stacked” estimator).  
We will also show results restricting to counties in the bottom half of 1960 per-capita income to ensure comparable need.

No running variable or cutoff is required (RDD not used).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. KEY IDENTIFYING ASSUMPTIONS  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Parallel trends: In the absence of CHCs, treated and control counties would have followed similar mortality trajectories.  
– Plausibility: Pre-period event-time coefficients should be flat; we can condition on county-specific linear trends and on 1960 demographic and economic covariates interacted with time.  

A2. No anticipation: Mortality does not change before the grant because residents foresee a CHC.  
– Plausibility: Funding decisions were finalized <12 months before opening and came as one-off OEO announcements, so long anticipatory health investments are unlikely. We still test for anticipatory effects in k = –5 .. –1.  

A3. SUTVA / no spillovers: A CHC in county i does not directly affect mortality in county j.  
– Plausibility: 1960s transportation costs and the mandate to serve local catchment areas limit cross-county patient flow. We will test for spillovers by excluding counties adjacent to treated ones.  

A4. Exogenous timing conditional on observables: After controlling for 1960 characteristics and state × year shocks, the exact year a county receives its CHC is as-good-as-random.  
– Historians’ accounts support the view that local activism, not time-varying mortality shocks, drove the queue. We will probe by regressing grant year on pre-1965 trends.  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. THREATS TO IDENTIFICATION & MITIGATIONS  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Targeting toward deteriorating health (“reverse causality”).  
• Fix: Include county-specific pre-trend in mortality (linear, or flexible spline), pre-period mortality level interacted with year FEs, and show that pre-trends are flat.  
• Placebo: Re-estimate using deaths from external causes unlikely to be affected by primary care (e.g., accidents) as a falsification test.  

T2. Confounding policies (Medicaid roll-out, hospital construction grants, physician supply).  
• Fix: Control for county-year Medicaid inpatient days, Medicare enrollment & outlays, AHA beds per capita, and state × year FEs; drop 1965–1966 transition years in robustness.  

T3. Compositional change (migration).  
• Fix: Use age-specific mortality rates with SEER denominator that updates intercensal counts rather than census enumeration; test for changes in population size/age structure; show that results are similar in age-adjusted rates.  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R CODE OUTLINE  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 0. Packages
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)     # fast data
library(fixest)         # DID & event-study
library(did)            # Callaway & Sant’Anna
library(ggplot2)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Load data
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
mort <- fread("mortality_county_year.csv")   # 1959–1988 mortality counts & pop
chc  <- fread("chc_grants.csv")             # county, first_grant_year
ctrl <- fread("county_controls_1960.csv")   # time-invariant controls
med  <- fread("medicare_medicaid_1967_88.csv")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Merge and construct variables
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
panel <- merge(mort, chc, by = "county_fips", all.x = TRUE)
panel <- merge(panel, med,  by = c("county_fips","year"), all.x = TRUE)
panel <- merge(panel, ctrl, by = "county_fips", all.x = TRUE)

# Treatment indicators
panel[, first_year := fifelse(is.na(first_grant_year), 9999, first_grant_year)]
panel[, treat        := as.integer(year >= first_year & first_year <= 1980)]
panel[, event_time   := year - first_year]           # negative for leads
panel[, ever_treated := as.integer(first_year <= 1980)]

# Event-time dummies for Sun & Abraham estimator
for(k in -10:15){
  panel[, paste0("e",k) := as.integer(event_time == k)]
}

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Main specification – Sun & Abraham event-study
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# We drop the implementation year (k = -1) as omitted baseline
es_formula <- death_rate ~ sunab(first_year, year) +
              medicare_pc + medicaid_pc + beds_per1000 +
              (pop60_poor + pop60_black)*factor(year)

main_fit <- feols(es_formula,
                  data = panel[year %between% c(1959,1988)],
                  fixef = ~ county_fips + year,
                  cluster = ~ county_fips)

# Aggregate ATT after 5+ years
att5 <- etable(main_fit, keep = "Sunab:>=5")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Callaway & Sant’Anna (robust to heterog.)
cs <- att_gt(yname = "death_rate",
             tname = "year",
             idname = "county_fips",
             gname = "first_year",
             xformla = ~ medicare_pc + medicaid_pc + beds_per1000,
             data    = panel[year %between% c(1959,1988) & first_year != 9999],
             control_group = "never")

agg_cs <- aggte(cs, type = "dynamic")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. Robustness: remove counties adjacent to treated
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
adj <- fread("contiguity_matrix.csv")  # county_i, county_j contiguous
adj_treated <- adj[county_j %in% chc$county_fips]
panel[, near_treat := county_fips %in% adj_treated$county_i]
robust_fit <- update(main_fit, subset = .(!near_treat))

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 6. Plot event-study coefficients
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
iplot(main_fit, ref.line = 0, xlab = "Years since first CHC", 
      main = "Event-study: CHCs and Age-adjusted Mortality")
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. EXPECTED RESULTS  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Prior: CHCs provided first-contact, low-cost care and prescriptions, especially hypertension and diabetes management. These chronic conditions disproportionately drive mortality among adults 50+. Therefore:  

• All-cause 50-74 mortality: expect a decline of 3–5 % (≈ 20–30 deaths per 100 000) within 5 years post-opening, growing to 5–7 % after 10 years.  
• Larger effects for ischemic heart disease and cerebrovascular deaths; negligible effects on accidents & cancers.  
• Infant mortality may fall modestly (<2 %) through improved prenatal care but Medicare focus is on older adults.  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. VALIDITY CHECKLIST SELF-ASSESSMENT (Difference-in-Differences)  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
C1: Well-defined treatment & timing ......................... 1  
C2: Parallel pre-trends demonstrated ........................ 1  
C3: No simultaneous policies biasing results ................ 0.5 (Medicaid/Medicare controlled but imperfect)  
C4: Stable composition / no migration bias .................. 0.5  
C5: No spillovers across control units ...................... 0.5  
TOTAL (out of 5) .......................................... 3.5  

The design is strong but relies on plausible rather than iron-clad assumptions about policy confounding, population mobility, and geographic spillovers.
